title: The Forest Can't Stand on the Ice
concept: A random forest of 100 decision trees, reading Sentinel-1 radar that sees through cloud and polar night, dated the ice on 30,774 North Slope lakes (Nguyen et al., The Cryosphere). On average ice went out around June 8th and came back around September 30th, about 114 open days, about 23 fewer days per degree north, and temperature led while shape and size added about 2 percent. The fair test: the 94 percent is agreement with clear-sky Sentinel-2 labels, not anyone on the ice, the paper says no field validation was done, and weather supplied most of the practice answers, though only for long deep cold or real warmth. The paper's temperature model matched the radar's dates for 82 and 75 percent of lakes, so the lakes that break the rule hold the next question, and a field check would settle it. Drawn as a troupe of faced decision trees punching up through the snow of a land where trees don't grow, voting ICE or WATER with ballot paddles, a thermometer teacher, an exam room on the shore with one empty desk on the ice, ducklings, and that empty desk alone on a fuchsia lake.

divergence_note: The last films were full rain-black night at one Juneau door with a faceless gunmetal letterbox and pencilled vellum (11-15), high-noon white sea ice with cobalt leads, a ringed seal and a survey camera (11-14), and a brass faucet with a face on an overcast gravel lot (11-13). This film is open tundra in three lights (polar night, midnight-sun honey, apricot dusk), its hero is a CROWD of soft wooden trees, not a single metal fixture, its AI colour is radar lime instead of cyan, and its world is the ground itself and the lakes in it. Honest overlaps: 11-14 also had a satellite and Arctic ice, answered by tundra lakes from the side and a crowd hero. 11-15 also opened at night, answered by keeping night to the first eight and last four seconds.

treatment.title: The Forest Can't Stand on the Ice
treatment.summary: Dramatist winner 'The Forest Can't Stand on the Ice', restaged at Gate 0. A troupe of faced decision trees (VoteTree, net-new) punches up through the snow of the North Slope, votes ICE or WATER with ballot paddles on one flagged kettle lake (ONE OF 30,774) per radar look, and a pressed lime label stamp MOST TREES LEAN ICE ripples across thousands of lakes. A thermometer on a wooden board deals weather-record practice cards; a 94% card's GRADED BY line hides under a flap. Act 2 is the midnight-sun summer of the findings (June 8th, September 30th, 114 days, 23 days per degree, a 2 percent tin cup, methane cut open by season). Act 3 is THE EXAM ROOM ON THE SHORE at dusk: the forest at desks in the sedge, the flap lifts to another satellite in a sun visor that only sees clear days, one empty teacher's desk slides out alone onto the lake ice, NO FIELD CHECK. From above, a ribbon of days shows the weather cards only at the deep-cold and real-warmth ends, the shoulder weeks filled by clear-sky cards and lime radar ticks. A logger at an instrumented lake pays out 80 TO 110 beside 114, different lakes and years. The turn lines twenty lakes up behind the thermometer like ducklings, about four step out glowing fuchsia (flagged for a field check), the tagged lake first, and the crane up shows about one in five across the slope. The radar's pixel view splits between shorelines and a lake that really differs, and the button leaves the empty desk alone on the fuchsia lake in polar night while the forest sinks into the snow on the shore and a caribou crosses behind.
treatment.judge_reasoning: Dramatist pitch won (49 of 60): the only full act structure with dated rehooks, a throughline lake that changes at every act boundary, a why-care beat and an Act 3 that tests then honestly narrows. Grafts: the Comedian's whack-a-mole open, tin cup, empty desk and duckling turn, the Explainer's report-card flip and whispering thermometer, the Enthusiast's June 8th mosquitoes. Fixes: no vote tallies, no named lake, the grader is clear-sky Sentinel-2 labels, averages say AVERAGE, shoreline is the paper's possibility, no boot prints at the unchecked lake.

angle.thesis: A random forest reading Sentinel-1 radar gave 30,774 North Slope lakes their first comprehensive ice calendar, through cloud and polar night, and that calendar mostly follows air temperature, so the lakes that break from it are where the next question lives, and a field check is what would settle it.
supporting_facts: Scale and sight: almost 31,000 lakes of 2 hectares or more, dated by a radar that needs no sun and sees through cloud, a look about every four days, read by a 100-tree random forest (c1, c3, c6, c7, c8).
The finding: about 23 fewer open-water days per degree north, and lake shape and size add only about 2 percent beyond temperature (c19, c21).
A simple temperature model matched the satellite ice-out dates for 82 percent of lakes and freeze-up for 75 percent, so the rest break from the simple rule (c23).
angle.counterpoint_to_honor: The 94 percent is agreement with clear-sky Sentinel-2 labels, not a field check, and the paper says no field validation was done (c13, c26). About 62 percent of the training labels came from weather records, so part of the temperature result leans on how the model was taught (c10), though those labels cover only long stretches of deep cold or real warmth. Earlier field work found 80 to 110 open days on instrumented lakes, short of this study's 114 average, different lakes and years, never called an error (c27, c18). The paper itself says some misfit lakes may reflect complex shorelines confusing the detector.
angle.falsifier: Field ice dates on instrumented North Slope lakes disagreeing with the radar dates by more than a couple of looks, or the lakes that break from the temperature rule turning out to be classifier errors rather than real outliers.

open_loop.what: Who stands on the ice? Planted when one tree's root taps the kettle lake's ice, cracks it and curls back, kept as the empty teacher's desk alone on the ice in the exam room while the forest sits on the shore, paid when the forest sinks into the snow under THE FOREST CAN'T STAND ON THE ICE and the empty desk waits on the lake NOT YET CHECKED.

open_loop_2.what: Who graded the 94 percent, and when can it see? Planted as a paper flap dropping over the card's GRADED BY line under WHO GRADED IT? while the voice says keep in mind who graded it, paid in the exam room on 'another satellite' when the flap lifts to a sun-visor satellite whose eye shuts each time a cloud drifts over, under SENTINEL-2 · CLEAR DAYS ONLY.
